chef_bio.background: Founded in 1860 (Man'en 1, the last year of the Edo period) on Kaminarimon-dori near Sensoji Temple, Owariya has been run by the same family for six generations across more than 160 years, serving Asakusa locals and Sensoji pilgrims. According to the shop's own account, the name comes from Shinmon Tatsugoro — the Edo-era fire brigade chief who also served as a gatekeeper of Sensoji — who suggested a name evoking the vigorous 'spread of a shrimp's tail' when the founder left firefighting to open the restaurant. The shop displays a 'Sensoji Goyo' (Official Purveyor to Sensoji Temple) sign, reflecting its long-standing ties to the temple.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop describes its aim as 'a flavor you don't tire of even eating it every day,' built on what it calls a trio of essentials: a bonito-based tsuyu, shrimp tempura fried in specially ordered sesame oil, and firm noodles made from top-grade domestic (Shinshu-centered) buckwheat flour.
chef_bio.specialty: Tempura soba (天ぷらそば) topped with two oversized shrimp tempura, fried in specially sourced sesame oil, so large they spill over the edge of the bowl

anecdotes.text: The novelist Nagai Kafu, a devoted Asakusa regular, is said to have eaten here every single day for a year. He always took the same reserved back seat, and the proprietress was instructed to serve him kashiwa nanban (chicken soba) without even taking his order once tea was poured. He ate in near-silence and left payment in coins lined up neatly along the edge of the table before leaving.

A photograph of Kafu eating at the restaurant — taken secretly by a fan, since the famously camera-shy writer disliked being photographed — was later given to the shop and still hangs inside as a memento of his patronage.

cultural_comfort.note: A famous, tourist-frequented shop steps from Sensoji with an English-language Tabelog listing, but no confirmed English menu — basic Japanese or pointing at the menu will help.

There is no mention of a dedicated fryer, gluten-free soy sauce, or allergy protocol. Not recommended for celiac diners without direct, in-person confirmation from staff.
tokyo_hakata_kushiyaki_yasaima.vegan_detail: This is a meat-focused izakaya whose signature dish is vegetables wrapped around domestic pork belly and grilled — the vegetables function as a wrapping for pork, not a standalone vegan dish. The rest of the menu (motsunabe offal hot pot, other pork/chicken skewers) is similarly meat-centered, and Japanese izakaya sauces/stocks routinely use bonito-based dashi. No vegan or vegetarian menu, labeling, or options were found in any source.

chef_bio.background: Goryon-san is operated by Basix Co. , Ltd. , a Tokyo restaurant group led by representative director Hiroshi Iwasawa (known as "Gan-san") that also runs the atmospheric izakaya brands Teyan-tei, Jomon, and Meatman. The Shibuya Miyamasuzaka branch opened on April 19 in a deliberately low-visibility spot — reached via a stairway down to a basement level with no prominent signage — reflecting the group's stated approach of building each shop's individuality around food and hospitality rather than location, signage, or a manual-driven service style.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's name, "Goryon-san," is a term of affection used in Hakata for a household's proprietress — a woman admired for her charm, virtue, kindness, and cooking skill during Hakata festivals. The restaurant frames its hospitality and cooking around that warm, home-style image.
chef_bio.specialty: Yasai-maki-gushi (野菜巻き串) — skewers of fresh vegetables wrapped in domestic pork belly and grilled; other signature items include steamed gyoza and Hakata motsunabe (offal hot pot).

anecdotes.text: The shop was deliberately opened on a quiet side street with no signage, reached down a basement stairway, as part of parent company Basix's philosophy of pursuing each shop's individual appeal through food and hospitality rather than location or manuals.

cultural_comfort.note: A standard Japanese-language izakaya chain outlet with no evidence of an English menu, picture menu, or foreign-visitor-oriented service — expect to order in Japanese or by pointing.

chef_bio.background: Before founding POTA PASTA, Ebato ran a Sanuki-udon specialty shop. He applied udon noodle-making techniques — 'fumikomi' (treading/kneading) and 'jukusei' (aging) — to durum wheat to develop a proprietary fresh pasta noodle, aiming to bring authentic hand-made-style pasta down to fast-food prices in a market he felt was stuck at roughly 1,000 yen per plate because dried pasta takes too long to cook for fast table turnover.
chef_bio.philosophy: Standardize every step — the fresh noodles and sauces are made off-site and flash-frozen, then simply boiled and combined to order — so that any staff member can consistently produce good pasta at very low prices (dishes historically started around 330–560 yen), making 'real' fresh pasta an everyday, fast-casual option near Shibuya Station.
chef_bio.specialty: Kiseki no Bolognese ("Miracle Bolognese") made with A4–A5 grade Japanese wagyu, and the shop's signature Ultimate Carbonara (究極のカルボナーラ) with a rich egg-and-cream sauce

anecdotes.text: Ebato developed the thick, chewy fresh pasta using know-how from his earlier Sanuki-udon shop, applying udon kneading and aging techniques to durum wheat as a proprietary product.

POTA PASTA was designed from the menu-development stage to fully standardize cooking so that any staff member makes the same dish — including a fully manualized method for the creamy egg-and-cream carbonara sauce.
The shop offers both thick and thin house-made noodles; the thick noodle is prized for its extra-chewy, edged mochi-mochi texture, the thin for how well it carries sauce.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is via a ticket vending machine with photo menus and no reservations needed, so pointing and basic numbers get you through even without English, but don't expect English-speaking staff for detailed allergy questions.

Diners choose from chicken, beef, shrimp, bean, or vegetable curry, and can dial the spice level up in steps (famously as high as 70x), which has made it a rite of passage for Tokyo spice enthusiasts as well as a lunchtime staple for office workers and students in the Jimbocho/Kanda area.

anecdotes.text: The shop opened in 1988 as a coffee-and-curry café; its name comes from an Ethiopian coffee blend that was popular with early customers.

Spice levels can be ordered far beyond standard, with regulars working their way up toward a legendary '70x' heat level over repeated visits.

General Japanese curry allergen guidance: soybean listing in a curry base commonly reflects soy sauce or Worcestershire sauce used as a hidden seasoning; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and is not gluten-free — a real, unmeasured gluten vector here.

positives.text: The curry roux is made without wheat flour, thickened naturally from a long-simmered puree of celery, onion, and other vegetables with 12 spices rather than a store-bought roux.

chef_bio.origin: Mita, Minato-ku, Tokyo (birthplace of the original Ramen Jiro honten)
chef_bio.background: Ramen Jiro traces its roots to a yatai (street stall) started around 1968 by Takami Yamada near Keio University in Mita, Minato-ku, which grew into the original honten (main shop) and, later, a network of independently run 'chokkei' (direct-lineage) branches trained in the founder's method. The Kabukicho shop opened on 1997-08-11 as a company-operated ('foods-kei') branch, and was uniquely permitted to keep the 'Jiro' name after the trademark was formally registered in 2003 (when other non-lineage branches had to drop it). In October 2016 it relocated to its current Kabukicho 2-chome address under new management and converted to full chokkei (direct-lineage) status, with an owner-chef trained in the Jiro method.
chef_bio.specialty: Jiro-style tonkotsu-shoyu ramen: thick, chewy flat noodles in a pork-bone and soy-sauce broth, topped with two slices of fatty chashu pork, garlic, and a towering mound of cabbage and bean sprouts, customizable via the shop's 'call' system (amount of garlic, vegetables, fat, and sauce strength).

anecdotes.text: Of the original company-run 'foods-kei' branches (which also included Shimbashi, Kanda, and Toranomon), the Kabukicho shop was the sole holdout allowed to keep operating under the 'Jiro' name after the 2003 trademark registration, until it converted to a true direct-lineage (chokkei) shop in 2016.
Staying open into the small hours (last order around 2:30am), the shop has become known as a late-night refuge in Kabukicho, drawing nightlife workers such as hosts and hostesses after their shifts.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth/tare is described as a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone and soy-sauce) base; standard Japanese soy sauce is wheat-based, and no wheat-free tamari alternative is mentioned anywhere.

chef_bio.origin: Shinjuku, Tokyo (founded 1954/opened as udon shop in 1965)
chef_bio.background: Sangokuichi traces back to 1954, when founder Hashimoto Ken went independent and opened a small (about 6-tsubo) shop near Shinjuku's east exit, first selling bags, then converting it into a ramen shop the following year. In 1965 the shop changed business again to become an udon restaurant. The name '三国一' ("best of the three kingdoms") comes from a trip: returning by shinkansen from a Sanuki-udon tasting tour in Shikoku, the founder saw Mt. Fuji through the train window — a peak visible from three provinces (Shizuoka, Kanagawa, Yamanashi) — and named the shop after it. The company now runs three shops around Shinjuku Station (east exit, west exit, and the Island Tower location), all still hand-making their own noodles.
chef_bio.philosophy: Everything made in-house: noodles are hand-pressed twice daily at the company's own nearby noodle-making facility and delivered fresh, and the dressing, mayonnaise, and dashi used across the menu are all made from scratch on site.
chef_bio.specialty: Salad udon (サラダうどん) — cold udon topped with fresh vegetables, tuna or meat, and a house-made mayonnaise-based dressing

anecdotes.text: The shop's name comes from the founder spotting Mt. Fuji — visible across three provinces — from a shinkansen window while returning from a Sanuki-udon eating trip in Shikoku.

Salad udon, now a common menu item at udon shops across Japan, is said to have originated here roughly 40 years ago when the previous-generation owner invented it during a health-food-conscious era; it became the shop's signature best-seller.
A food writer compared the shop's cult following and hearty, no-frills style to Ramen Jiro, calling it 'the Jiro of udon.'

cultural_comfort.note: An old-school, mostly local udon shop near Shinjuku Station West Exit; a Tabelog English page and delivery-app listing exist, but basic Japanese or pointing at the menu will help.

chef_bio.origin: Founded 2004 in a tiny 4-tsubo, 8-seat rented space in Shinjuku Golden Gai
chef_bio.background: Ramen Nagi began in 2004 when founder Satoshi Ikuta and ramen-loving friends started serving noodles once a week out of a borrowed, tiny Golden Gai space with no money, no signature flavor, and no customers. The shop's name, Nagi (凪, meaning a windless calm sea), was chosen because the founders felt they had nothing to start with and wanted to create their own wind from a calm sea. Word of mouth grew the weekly pop-up into a full-time shop, and lines eventually stretched over 100 people deep outside this same Golden Gai alley. This location is the original honkan (main store) where the entire Nagi niboshi-ramen chain began, and it has since grown into a chain of 40+ locations in Japan and dozens more overseas.
chef_bio.philosophy: Nagi's ethos is built around pushing niboshi (dried fish) ramen to its most concentrated, umami-heavy extreme, and around the shop's scrappy, community-built origin story in Golden Gai's tiny alleys.
chef_bio.specialty: Sugoi Niboshi Ramen — a intensely rich broth built from dried niboshi (baby sardines/anchovies), sourced from producers across Japan, combined with an original wide "ittan-men" noodle and a spiced sardine-based tare aged for several days.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name was chosen at a low point: with no money, no signature taste, and no customers, the founders decided to make their own "wind" from Nagi, a windless calm sea.
In 2015, this Golden Gai shop briefly collaborated with insect-food advocate Yuta Shinohara on a limited 100-bowl "cricket ramen," using dried cricket for dashi alongside the usual niboshi.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature tare is a spiced sardine (iwashi)-based sauce; standard Japanese ramen tare of this type is soy-sauce based and contains wheat, though no source explicitly confirmed wheat content for this specific shop's tare.

cultural_comfort.note: A famous, tourist-visited Golden Gai landmark with an English Tabelog listing and ticket-vending-machine ordering, but menus and staff interaction are primarily in Japanese.

chef_bio.philosophy: A jingisukan (spiced, herb-marinated grilled lamb) specialist by night who uses the quiet weekday lunch hours to recreate the nostalgic roadside tonkotsu ramen of his Nagasaki youth
chef_bio.specialty: Kyushu-style (Nagahama/Hakata) tonkotsu ramen served only on weekday lunches, made with a pork-head-based broth continually replenished (yobimodashi method) alongside a spine/knuckle stock for a rich, emulsified, lightly funky ('kusa-uma') pork-bone flavor without excess gaminess

anecdotes.text: The lunch ramen was born as a side project by the jingisukan chef: he set out to reproduce the funky-but-delicious ('kusa-uma') pork-bone ramen from old Nagahama ramen stalls, simmering a pork-head-based stock and continually replenishing it with backbone/knuckle stock (a traditional 'yobimodashi' method) so the broth turns rich and lightly emulsified without becoming too gamey.
Reviewers describe being surprised that a jingisukan specialty shop could turn out ramen of this quality, calling it a genuine hidden find rather than a side-business afterthought.

cultural_comfort.note: A very local, characterful spot (playful pun name, jingisukan-by-night/ramen-by-day setup) with no confirmed English menu or signage, so some comfort navigating Japanese-only ordering is helpful.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The salad bar is a shared self-serve buffet where guests use common serving utensils across all dishes, so cross-contact between gluten-containing and gluten-free items is possible even though many items are naturally gluten-free.

Sizzler Shinjuku Mitsui Building (a different, nearby branch) is described as 'not a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease' — no branch has celiac-grade confirmation, including this one.

Chain-level assessment: 'As a chain restaurant, Sizzler typically means a high risk of cross-contact, and it is likely not possible to dine safely at this establishment if you have celiac disease or must avoid cross-contact.' A manager reportedly said only 'a couple of items in the salad bar' are gluten-free and those are 'subject to cross contamination,' and reviewers 'wouldn't trust the salad because of so much cross contamination.'

Salad-bar croutons are wheat-flour bread fried in oil; unpackaged buffet dishes carry no labeling obligation and even trace exposure can trigger symptoms, so wheat-allergic/celiac diners must confirm cross-contamination directly with staff — i.e. the buffet is a documented cross-contact hazard, not a safe self-serve GF environment.

staff_allergy_handling.text: General reporting on the Sizzler Japan chain describes staff providing an allergen-removal menu and a list covering 25+ designated allergen items on request, though this describes chain-wide practice rather than a confirmation specific to the Shinjuku Toho Building branch.

A Tripadvisor review of a different Tokyo Sizzler branch (Setagaya) reported staff bringing an allergy-information folder when asked, suggesting this is a chain-standard practice, though not independently confirmed for this Shinjuku location.

positives.text: The salad bar is described as offering 70+ items of fresh seasonal vegetables, fruit, and made-to-order components, giving diners with dietary restrictions substantial control over what goes on their own plate.

cultural_comfort.note: A major hotel-based chain restaurant (inside Hotel Gracery Shinjuku) catering heavily to domestic and international/tourist guests, with online reservation booking and a self-explanatory buffet format that needs little Japanese to navigate.

chef_bio.background: Ramen Tatsunoya (龍の家) was founded in Kurume, Fukuoka in 1999 by staff who had trained at Hakata's famed Ippudo. The Shinjuku Otakibashi-dori branch began life in September 2007 as a stall in the Tobu Department Store Ikebukuro ramen food court before relocating to its current roadside spot on Otakibashi-dori on July 11, 2009 — the brand's first standalone Kanto shop. The chain has since grown to about a dozen locations across Kyushu, Tokyo, and overseas, and this Shinjuku shop sits among the neighborhood's ramen heavyweights (Ramen Jiro, Ichiran, Menya Musashi, Mongoru Tanmen Nakamoto).
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than following the traditional Kurume 'yobimodoshi' method of continuously topping up the tonkotsu stock, Tatsunoya uses a 'torikiri' approach, cooking down and using up each day's broth in full. The brand describes its style as 'Neo Kurume ramen' — noodles 'born in Hakata, raised in Kurume. '
chef_bio.specialty: Tsukemen motsu — offal (motsu) dipping noodles in a pork-bone base, an item exclusive to this Tokyo shop — alongside the shop's core tonkotsu ramen made from pork bones simmered into a rich, mild-flavored soup.

chef_bio.background: Katsumi was founded in 1976 (Showa 51) by the current owner's father as a neighborhood kappo restaurant near Dogenzaka-ue. Tsuda Katsuyuki, born in 1975, grew up watching his father cook and naturally set his sights on becoming a chef himself. He trained at Kaiseki Kawabata and Hanagoyomi in Roppongi before joining the family restaurant, and became the second-generation owner in 2009 when his father retired.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tsuda goes to Tsukiji himself every morning to hand-select fish, and the kitchen emphasizes simple, ingredient-forward washoku built on traditional kappo fundamentals rather than novelty.
chef_bio.specialty: きんき煮付 (simmered kinki/thornhead rockfish) — the restaurant's most popular dish, prepared in an old-fashioned, gently sweet-savory style; the lunchtime oyakodon (chicken-and-egg rice bowl) is also a well-known specialty.

毎日店主が築地に出向き、目利きを働かせて仕入れた鮮度の良い魚を6〜7品盛り合わせた豪華な一皿を提供している。一番人気は「きんき煮付」で、昔ながらの優しい味が名物料理となっている。
昭和51年創業の歴史ある味を800円から提供 — restaurant opened in Showa 51 (1976) and is known for its long-standing, affordable lunch dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional neighborhood kappo restaurant run by a Japanese-speaking family; no evidence of an English menu or English-speaking staff was found, so first-timers should expect a Japanese-only experience.

The Dogenzaka shop opened in 1935, and the fruit parlor on its 2nd floor was added the following year, 1936. Today the 1st floor houses the flagship fruit shop selling premium seasonal fruit for gifts and personal use, while the 2nd-floor parlor serves fruit parfaits and fruit sandwiches, one minute's walk from Shibuya Station's Hachiko exit, just past the Scramble Crossing.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen prizes each fruit at its seasonal peak, changing the menu roughly seven times a year so parfaits and sandwiches always feature fruit at its best.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal fruit sandwich (フルーツサンド) and fruit parfaits built around whichever fruits are in peak season

anecdotes.text: Founded in 1910 as a high-end fruit shop; the Dogenzaka store opened in 1935 with the parlor added in 1936. The menu is changed about seven times a year to serve fruit at its most delicious moment.
The 'Special Seasonal Fruit Sandwich,' combining Tochiotome strawberries with mixed fruit across two sandwich types, is a signature item at roughly 1,880 yen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or process was documented; wheat-containing bread and cake components are used throughout the parfait and sandwich menu.

positives.text: Fresh, high-quality seasonal fruit is the centerpiece of every dish, giving naturally gluten-free and plant-based components (the fruit itself) even though prepared dishes are not GF/vegan overall.

cultural_comfort.note: English menus are available and the spot is a well-known tourist stop right off Shibuya Scramble Crossing, but staff English is limited, so a few basic Japanese phrases help.

Tempura sides (self-served from a shared counter) are fried in a shared fryer alongside wheat-battered items, and shoyu-based dipping sauces are standard. No dedicated fryer, dedicated gluten-free prep area, or staff allergy protocol was found. Not suitable for a celiac or wheat-allergic diner.

No vegan or dashi-free option, plant-based menu, or vegan labeling was found in any source. Dry/tossed styles like bukkake or zaru with soy-based tare might reduce but not eliminate animal-derived ingredients (shoyu-based tare can itself contain bonito extract), and this was not confirmed either way — not recommended for a strict vegan diner without asking staff directly (Japanese-only environment).

chef_bio.philosophy: Bring the real, no-frills self-service Sanuki udon experience to Tokyo — order your noodles, help yourself to tempura and sides from the counter, and pay at the register at the end, just as at the honke (originator) shops in Kagawa.
chef_bio.specialty: Kake udon finished with iriko (dried-sardine) dashi poured from a self-serve tap on the wall, and the shop's popular mentai kama-tama udon (mentaiko and raw egg tossed with hot noodles).

anecdotes.text: Diners pour their own iriko dashi from a tap mounted on the wall before eating, part of the shop's deliberately rustic, self-service Sanuki-style setup.

The shop is the second Tokyo offshoot of the original "Mentsudan" group, opened in July 2009 by a Kagawa-native manager who had previously run the Nishi-Shinjuku Tokyo Mentsudan and the Kichijoji branch.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shop's signature broth is iriko dashi, made from dried sardines/anchovies — a fish-based stock used throughout the menu, not a vegan option.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a self-service Sanuki udon shop: order and receive your noodles first, help yourself to tempura and side dishes from the counter, then pay at the register — the multi-step flow can be confusing on a first visit, but pointing at the picture menu works fine.

tokyo_kushiyaki_ishikawa.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free protocol or menu was found. As a tare-based kushiyaki shop, the standard basting sauce is soy-sauce based (contains wheat), and tsukune (chicken meatballs) commonly use a wheat-based binder. Ordering skewers shio (salt-grilled, no tare) would reduce but not eliminate wheat exposure, since the same charcoal/electric grill and tare-brushing tools are shared across items. Celiac-level diners should ask staff directly and treat this as a use-caution, not a confirmed-safe, option.
tokyo_kushiyaki_ishikawa.vegan_detail: The menu is built entirely around Oyama-dori chicken (sashimi and grilled skewers); no vegetarian or vegan dishes were identified in any source. Not a suitable choice for vegan diners.

chef_bio.philosophy: Built around a single high-quality chicken breed (Oyama-dori) and careful skewer-by-skewer grilling rather than a sprawling menu.

anecdotes.text: Skewers start from around 150 yen — inexpensive for the Shinjuku area — with a typical dinner running about 4,000-4,999 yen.
The restaurant is known for its chicken sashimi from Oyama-dori chicken, dressed simply with wasabi, as its signature dish.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local izakaya with a Japanese-language menu and no evidence of English-speaking service, though its Tabelog listing does have an English page for browsing before you go.

tokyo_benten.gf_detail: No gluten-free noodles or dedicated preparation are mentioned anywhere. This is a traditional Edo-style soba-ya; the noodles are standard soba (not confirmed as 100%/juwari buckwheat), the dipping sauce (tsuyu) is soy-sauce based, and the menu includes tempura. No source mentions a gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or celiac accommodation — not a safe choice for strict gluten-free diners.

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood soba shop in Asakusa's Kannon-ura backstreets, founded in 1950. It closed temporarily for seismic reinforcement and renovation work and reopened in March 2026, continuing to serve the same backstreet clientele it always has.
chef_bio.philosophy: A longtime regular describes the shop's ethos as unpretentious: soba here is everyday comfort food, best enjoyed simply — soba shochu cut with soba-yu (noodle cooking water) alongside a few small dishes, finished with a plate of noodles, rather than a ceremonious affair.
chef_bio.specialty: Hamaguri seiro — clam dipping soba with plump, briny hamaguri clams. Originally offered only in spring, it proved so popular that it became a year-round fixture. Seasonal specialties include kaki nanban (oyster soba) in winter and nishin soba (herring soba).

anecdotes.text: A writer recalls being taken to Benten by his grandfather and describes it as a tiny, spotlessly kept shop seating only about a dozen people, where the ritual is soba-yu-wari (soba shochu diluted with the noodles' cooking water) with small dishes before the soba itself — soba, he writes, 'shouldn't be eaten pretentiously, just as everyday comfort food.'
The clam dipping soba (hamaguri seiro) began as a spring-only special but became so popular with regulars that it is now served year-round.
Founded in 1950, the shop closed for seismic reinforcement and renovation work and reopened on March 5, 2026.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional local soba-ya with no confirmed English menu and cash-only payment — an authentic neighborhood experience rather than a tourist-oriented one.

chef_bio.background: The owner was born and raised on Aogashima, a remote volcanic island in the Izu chain with a population of roughly 160 people. The restaurant opened in Nishi-Shinjuku on March 24, 2014, bringing island food and drink to the mainland for people who cannot easily make the difficult boat/helicopter trip to Aogashima itself.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithfully reproduces Aogashima and wider Izu/Ogasawara island home cooking in Tokyo, using seafood, vegetables, salt and shochu sourced from the islands rather than mainland substitutes.
chef_bio.specialty: Aogashima and Izu-island regional dishes such as simmered sea turtle, muro-aji (mackerel scad) fish cutlet, and ashitaba (island celery) with tuna mayonnaise, alongside the island's rare 'ao-chu' shochu.

anecdotes.text: The owner's family runs a minshuku (guesthouse) back on Aogashima and is also involved in producing the island's rare 'ao-chu' shochu, which the restaurant pours in Tokyo.

The restaurant is described as a way to experience Aogashima's isolated island culture and cuisine without leaving West Shinjuku, complete with an aerial photo of the island marking the building entrance.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locally-run izakaya with a Japanese-language menu and standard izakaya service style; English support is not documented, so some Japanese phrasebook or translation help is useful.

chef_bio.philosophy: No-frills, fast-fried tempura at old-Tokyo teishoku-ya prices, served at a worn wooden counter with a deliberately retro Showa-era feel rather than a polished dining-out experience

anecdotes.text: Founder Miyata's family had sold daigaku-imo (candied sweet potato) before he opened the tempura shop in 1959 — the shop kept the 'imo' (potato) name even after the switch to tempura.

The original honten ran for roughly 60 years on just 7 counter seats, with lines forming at lunchtime, before closing for good on March 31, 2018; several branch shops (noren-wake) continued the recipes afterward.

chef_bio.specialty: Junten-nen dashi ramen — a completely no-chemical-seasoning (無化調), 100% natural-ingredient ramen built on a seafood-and-chicken dashi (bonito, dried sardine, chicken) finished with a house-rendered lard-and-sesame aroma oil and a hint of rayu chili heat.

anecdotes.text: Kanegae first opened a ramen shop called Shima Ramen Masashiya in Naha, Okinawa in 2008, naming it 'Masashi' after the owner of a guesthouse (minshuku) he loved staying at during his time in Okinawa.

In 2011 he and his wife moved the business to Tokyo, opening in the current Minamidaira, Shibuya location under the name Art Masashiya — the 'Art' chosen in tribute to Art Coffee Salon, the kissaten (retro coffee shop) that had operated in the same space for more than 20 years before them.
The shop keeps much of the original kissaten's interior intact, giving the ramen counter a nostalgic, Showa-era coffee-shop atmosphere rather than a typical ramen-shop look.

cultural_comfort.note: A hidden, retro-café-turned-ramen-counter with a cash-only Japanese ticket vending machine and no English menu, so a little Japanese (or a translation app) helps, though the counter staff are described as friendly to newcomers.

tokyo_gazzo.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free menu, wheat-free pasta/bread substitution, or dedicated fryer was found on the restaurant's own pages or major booking sites. The kitchen is pasta- and bread-forward (Italian) and uses a shared charcoal grill and open counter kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat is likely. Sauces lean on imported spices/herbs/citrus rather than Japanese soy-based sauces, which may reduce (but not eliminate) hidden-wheat risk from shoyu/dashi common at Japanese-style restaurants; this was not explicitly confirmed either way. Celiac diners should call ahead and confirm specific dishes and cooking surfaces.
tokyo_gazzo.vegan_detail: GAZZO's identity is built around a butcher-shop/charcoal-grilled-meat concept ('spice x butcher's'), with organic vegetables used as accompaniments rather than as a standalone vegan menu. No vegan-specific dishes, plant-based substitutions, or confirmation of meat-stock-free sauces were found. Vegan diners should call ahead to ask which vegetable dishes can be made without meat, butter, or animal-based stock.
tokyo_gazzo.hours_raw: Lunch Mon-Fri 11:30-14:30 (L.O. 14:00); Dinner Mon-Thu & Sat 18:00-21:30 (L.O.), Fri 18:00-22:00 (L.O.); Sunday/holidays normally closed but can open irregularly for pre-booked parties of 10+.
tokyo_gazzo.notes: The chef trained originally as a dolce (pastry) craftsman before shifting to charcoal-grilled Italian cooking, which shows up in the restaurant's habit of presenting handmade cakes to guests celebrating birthdays and anniversaries. · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

chef_bio.chef_name: "Tecchan" (てっちゃん), referred to on the restaurant's own materials as the 'good-mood chef'
chef_bio.background: The chef trained originally as a dolce (pastry) craftsman before shifting to charcoal-grilled Italian cooking, which shows up in the restaurant's habit of presenting handmade cakes to guests celebrating birthdays and anniversaries.
chef_bio.philosophy: The stated house motto is 'Umai! ga seikai' ("Delicious is the only right answer") — cooking meat simply over charcoal to let the ingredient quality speak, rather than heavy technique or formal fine-dining pretension.
chef_bio.specialty: Whole cuts of carefully selected meat (from contracted domestic farms) grilled simply over charcoal and finished with dozens of imported spices, herbs, and citrus, alongside organic-vegetable side dishes.

anecdotes.text: The chef, a former pastry craftsman, personally makes and presents handmade cakes to guests dining for a birthday or anniversary.
The restaurant frames its cooking as 'spice x butcher's,' grilling whole cuts of contract-farm meat over charcoal and finishing them with spices, herbs, and citrus gathered from around the world.

positives.text: The kitchen sources organic vegetables and uses fresh, traceable contract-farm meat, and cooking relies mainly on charcoal grilling plus imported spices/herbs/citrus rather than heavy sauces, which may make it easier to identify and discuss individual allergens with staff.

cultural_comfort.note: No English menu or English-speaking staff could be confirmed online; phone reservations (03-6661-2150) and ordering are expected to be in Japanese, so a translation app is recommended.

tokyo_teuchi_soba_fujiya.gf_detail: The shop offers 十割そば (juwari, 100% buckwheat noodles with no wheat flour in the noodle itself) as an upgrade from its standard 二八そば (80% buckwheat / 20% wheat blend), so a wheat-free noodle option exists. However, no dedicated gluten-free kitchen, fryer, or boiling water is documented; the shop also serves wheat-battered tempura and likely uses standard soy-sauce-based tsuyu, and both juwari and nihachi noodles are hand-made in the same space. This is not confirmed celiac-safe — cross-contact risk is real and unmanaged as far as published sources show; ask staff directly before ordering.
tokyo_teuchi_soba_fujiya.vegan_detail: No vegan menu, dashi ingredients, or vegetarian accommodations are documented for this shop. Traditional soba tsuyu (dipping sauce) is conventionally bonito/katsuobushi dashi-based, and nothing in available sources indicates a plant-based alternative here.
tokyo_teuchi_soba_fujiya.hours_raw: 11:30〜売り切れまで（14時前後）、17:30〜21:00 L.O.（土曜・日曜・祝日休み）
tokyo_teuchi_soba_fujiya.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop traces its lineage to Kashiwagi Fujiya (柏木ふじ家), a Nishi-Shinjuku soba shop founded in 1933. chef_bio.origin: Nishi-Shinjuku, Tokyo
chef_bio.background: The shop traces its lineage to Kashiwagi Fujiya (柏木ふじ家), a Nishi-Shinjuku soba shop founded in 1933. After that original shop closed, its fourth-generation successor — who had trained at Tokyo shops recognized with a Michelin Bib Gourmand, including Soba Tajima in Hiroo and Honjinbo in Shinbashi — opened this reincarnation, Teuchi Soba Fujiya, in December 2019, later moving to its current Nishi-Shinjuku Daikyo Building location to refine the hand-made soba further.
chef_bio.philosophy: Everything from milling the domestically-sourced buckwheat on a stone mill to hand-cutting the noodles is done in-house without machines, and noodles are boiled to order just before serving for the best texture and aroma.
chef_bio.specialty: 十割そば (juwari soba, 100% buckwheat noodles), hand-ground on a custom stone mill and hand-cut without machines, served alongside freshly fried tempura.

anecdotes.text: The owner personally hand-grinds buckwheat with a special stone mill and hand-cuts every noodle without machines, a discipline carried over from training at Michelin Bib Gourmand-listed Tokyo soba shops.

The restaurant is the fourth-generation continuation of the old Nishi-Shinjuku shop Kashiwagi Fujiya (founded 1933); the current owner reopened it under the new name in December 2019 after training at Soba Tajima (Hiroo) and Honjinbo (Shinbashi).

gf_cross_contamination.text: The restaurant's menu structure offers a 100% buckwheat (juwari) noodle alongside its standard wheat-blended (nihachi) noodle, but no dedicated gluten-free prep area, fryer, or cooking water is documented, and tempura is wheat-battered.

汁は良質な本節からとった出汁とかえしを合わせています (The tsuyu combines dashi taken from quality honbushi/dried bonito with kaeshi) — confirms both a non-vegan bonito dashi AND a wheat-soy-sauce kaeshi in the sauce served with all noodles, including juwari.
gf_cross_contamination.source: https://soba-fujiya.jp/ (shop's own description, quoted in web search snippets)

gf_cross_contamination.text: ベースの蕎麦は二八そばですが、十割そばに変更することも可能です (The base soba is nihachi/80-20 wheat blend, but it can be changed to juwari) — the default product contains wheat; juwari is only an upgrade swap made in the same hand-cutting operation.

Restaurant offers hand-made 100% buckwheat soba AND crispy wheat-battered tempura in the same small shop; multiple listings describe no gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer, and no allergen-handling information.

General guidance: 'many dried and fresh versions of soba noodles in Japan are nonetheless mixed with wheat' and soba shops routinely use wheat-soy tsuyu and shared boiling water — celiacs are advised to confirm directly; no source documents Fujiya doing any of this safely.

positives.text: A wheat-free (100% buckwheat) noodle option is a standing menu item rather than a special request, which is a meaningful GF-aware baseline compared to shops offering only wheat-blended soba.

cultural_comfort.note: Traditional local soba craftsman's shop with an all-Japanese menu and no confirmed English signage or menu, though modern cashless payment (card, e-money, QR pay) is accepted.

tokyo_thali_ya_shibuya_namikib.gf_detail: The signature format centers on wheat naan baked fresh in-house with free refills, but rice can be substituted as the base, which removes the naan itself from the meal. However, no information was found confirming the curries are made without a wheat-based roux/thickener or wheat-containing soy sauce, and the open kitchen actively rolls and bakes wheat naan throughout service, creating a real flour cross-contamination risk. There is no evidence of a dedicated gluten-free process, so this is not a safe default choice for celiac diners without direct confirmation from staff.
tokyo_thali_ya_shibuya_namikib.vegan_detail: The set-meal format lets you pick 2 curries from a rotating list that typically includes a vegetable curry alongside chicken, keema, and mutton options, but the vegetable curry is not confirmed to be free of ghee, butter, or cream, which are common in Japanized Indian curry gravies. No dedicated vegan menu, labeling, or preparation process was found for this location, so vegan diners should ask staff about dairy/ghee in the specific curry before ordering.
tokyo_thali_ya_shibuya_namikib.notes: Thali-ya (ターリー屋) is one of Japan's largest Indian-curry chains, launched in 2002 in Tokyo and since expanded to roughly 44 shops across Tokyo, Kanagawa, Chiba, and Osaka. This Shibuya branch sits right at the Namikibashi intersection on Meiji-dori, on the walk from Shibuya Statio · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

roles: chain restaurant / branch of a Tokyo-founded Indian curry chain
chef_bio.origin: Tokyo, Japan (chain founded 2002)
chef_bio.background: Thali-ya (ターリー屋) is one of Japan's largest Indian-curry chains, launched in 2002 in Tokyo and since expanded to roughly 44 shops across Tokyo, Kanagawa, Chiba, and Osaka. This Shibuya branch sits right at the Namikibashi intersection on Meiji-dori, on the walk from Shibuya Station toward Ebisu.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chain built its identity by moving away from the idea that Indian food in Japan means only 'curry rice,' instead creating a distinct 'Indian teishoku (set meal)' category — one-plate meals meant to fill you up, with unlimited naan refills and free large-portion rice.
chef_bio.specialty: The ターリー屋定食 (Thali-ya set meal): a choice of two curries served with tandoori items and freshly baked naan (with free refills) or rice, in generous, filling portions.

anecdotes.text: A visiting blogger described the shop's cramped, narrow interior as part of its charm, and singled out the tandoori set meal as tasting notably good.
The shop is noted for a dedicated takeout counter where customers can order curry-and-naan or curry-and-rice bento boxes directly from outside.

cultural_comfort.note: A Japanese-run chain Indian-curry shop primarily oriented to local diners; no confirmed English menu or English-speaking service for this branch, though the picture-friendly curry-and-naan set format is easy to point-and-order even without Japanese.

tokyo_tachigui_soba_kamu_stand.gf_detail: This is a conventional standing-soba shop, not a gluten-free or buckwheat-only (juwari) specialist — its signature noodle is explicitly described as an extra-thick, wheat-blended "wasshiwashi" style, and traditional soba tsuyu/dipping sauce at this type of shop is wheat-based shoyu tare. No gluten-free noodle, sauce, or dedicated-fryer accommodation was found in any source. Not recommended for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
tokyo_tachigui_soba_kamu_stand.vegan_detail: The shop's specialty is a meat dipping soba with a choice of beef, pork, or chicken, and no vegan-specific menu items were found in any source. Standing-soba tsuyu at shops of this type is typically built on bonito (katsuo)-based dashi. Not recommended for vegan diners.
tokyo_tachigui_soba_kamu_stand.notes: [Mom & Pop] Opened May 7, 2025 on Hakusan-dori between Jimbocho and Suidobashi stations, the shop quickly drew attention from Tokyo's tachigui-soba (standing soba) enthusiast community for noodles far thicker and chewier than the typical standing-soba norm. · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

roles: Standing soba shop specializing in extra-thick, chewy noodles
chef_bio.background: Opened May 7, 2025 on Hakusan-dori between Jimbocho and Suidobashi stations, the shop quickly drew attention from Tokyo's tachigui-soba (standing soba) enthusiast community for noodles far thicker and chewier than the typical standing-soba norm.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's own name, Kamu (嚙む, "to chew"), states its concept outright: noodles thick and firm enough that eating them means real chewing rather than the usual soba slurp, which reviewers say releases more of the buckwheat's aroma and flavor with each bite.
chef_bio.specialty: Meat dipping soba (nikutsuke soba) — choice of beef, pork, or chicken piled over extra-thick 'wasshiwashi' noodles, alongside tempura soba and a limited-time soba breakfast (6:00-9:00).

anecdotes.text: The regular price for the meat dipping soba is 980 yen; for the opening days of May 7-10, 2025 it was offered at a 300-yen discount (680 yen).
Reviewers describe the noodles as 'wasshiwashi' style, thick with strong chew, calling it true to the shop's chew-focused name.
The interior is a chic, black-toned, clean design meant to feel calm enough that women dining alone are comfortable there.

cultural_comfort.note: Standing-only counter shop that orders via a Japanese-language ticket vending machine (shokken), typical of tachigui-soba stalls, with no English menu reported.

tokyo_gensoba_shingari_asakusa.vegan_detail: The menu is built around animal proteins (wagyu beef, shrimp tempura, horse sashimi) and the standard tsuyu dipping sauce for the soba is very likely made with bonito (katsuo) dashi, per general soba-restaurant convention and the restaurant's own menu descriptions. No vegan option, dashi substitution, or plant-based dipping sauce was found in any available source, so this cannot be recommended as vegan-friendly.
tokyo_gensoba_shingari_asakusa.hours_raw: 10:00〜22:00（L.O. 21:00）の通し営業。休日前日（金曜日を除く）は〜22:30まで延長。無休。
tokyo_gensoba_shingari_asakusa.notes: [Mom & Pop] 浅草寺に近い新仲見世通り沿いで営業する玄蕎麦（皮ごと挽いた蕎麦粉を使う蕎麦）の専門店。株式会社ココチーノが運営し、埼玉県草加市にもう一店舗を持つ小規模な2店舗展開。

roles: 蕎麦専門店（十割玄蕎麦・天ぷら）
chef_bio.origin: 浅草・新仲見世通り（浅草寺近く）で営業する玄蕎麦専門店。埼玉県草加市にもう1店舗を構える小規模2店舗展開。
chef_bio.background: 浅草寺に近い新仲見世通り沿いで営業する玄蕎麦（皮ごと挽いた蕎麦粉を使う蕎麦）の専門店。 株式会社ココチーノが運営し、埼玉県草加市にもう一店舗を持つ小規模な2店舗展開。
chef_bio.philosophy: つなぎを使わない完全十割にこだわり、蕎麦粉を自家製粉、麺は注文が入ってから打つ。 蕎麦つゆに添える辛味大根も店主自らが栽培したものを使うなど、自家生産・自家製粉・打ちたてを軸にした蕎麦作りを掲げている。
chef_bio.specialty: 完全十割玄蕎麦 — つなぎ粉を一切使わず、国産玄蕎麦粉100%だけで打った蕎麦。 新潟県・長野県の契約農家から仕入れた在来種の玄そばを店主自身が石臼で挽き、注文後にその都度製麺するという打ちたてにこだわる。

anecdotes.text: 店主自ら新潟県・長野県の契約農家から仕入れた在来種のみの玄そばを石臼で挽き、蕎麦つゆに添える辛味大根も自家栽培している。
その時期最高の国内産玄蕎麦粉を100%使い、注文後に製麺する完全十割蕎麦を、浅草寺・浅草駅近くの新仲見世通り沿いで通し営業（10:00〜22:00）で提供している。

gf_cross_contamination.text: The soba is 完全十割 (100% domestic whole buckwheat flour, no wheat binder), confirmed across multiple sources, but tempura using a wheat-flour batter is prepared in the same kitchen and no dedicated fryer or gluten-free handling protocol was confirmed.
Celiac reviewer notes that while the soba noodles are 100% buckwheat, the broth/tsuyu isn't gluten free; a customer who asked to have a meal made without soy sauce was told no.

Review content surfaced via aggregator listing: staff made sure not to include soya (often containing wheat) in the soup for one celiac guest — indicating accommodation is ad hoc and inconsistent, not a documented protocol.

Shop's own menu lists shrimp tempura, large-shrimp tempura, and kakiage (wheat-battered fried items) alongside 十割 soba, confirming an on-premises wheat fryer and cross-contamination exposure; no GF/allergen accommodation stated.
Menu items include 黒毛和牛すき玄蕎麦 (kuroge wagyu), 海老天 (shrimp tempura), 馬刺し (horse sashimi), 湯葉刺し (yuba) — an animal-protein-centric menu with conventional katsuo-dashi tsuyu, no vegan option found.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No source confirmed whether the tsuyu (dipping sauce) uses a wheat-free soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and this has not been verified as gluten-free at this restaurant.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is centered on animal proteins (wagyu beef, shrimp tempura, horse sashimi) and the tsuyu dipping sauce is very likely made with bonito (katsuo) dashi; no vegan-adapted dish or dashi substitution was found in available sources.

positives.text: The base soba noodle is a genuine 100% buckwheat (juwari) product milled in-house from single-origin buckwheat and cut fresh per order, rather than a machine-made 2:8 blend that always contains wheat.
positives.source_wording: What the page actually says: 「その時期最高の国内産玄蕎麦粉(玄粉100%)を使った完全十割蕎麦。注文後に製麺する打ちたて」 — top-grade seasonal DOMESTIC whole-buckwheat flour, noodles EXTRUDED/CUT after you order.

cultural_comfort.note: Sits directly on Asakusa's tourist-heavy Shin-Nakamise shopping street near Sensoji, so some visitor familiarity is likely, but no English menu or multilingual staff was confirmed in available sources.

tokyo_raoma_hinabebou.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, certification, or explicit wheat-free claim was found. The broths themselves (pork-bone/chicken-carcass base with Chinese herbs) do not have confirmed wheat content, but Chinese hot pot dipping sauces and seasonings commonly contain wheat-based soy sauce or bean pastes, and this was not addressed on any source checked. Diners with celiac disease should ask staff directly about the composition of the dipping sauce, broth seasonings, and any shared cooking surfaces before ordering.
tokyo_raoma_hinabebou.vegan_detail: Both signature broths (the mild white broth and the numbing mala broth) are made from an 8-hour pork-bone and chicken-carcass stock, so neither is vegan or vegetarian regardless of which vegetables are chosen. Over 30 vegetable varieties are kept in stock and could be ordered as ingredients, but no vegetable-only or vegan broth option, and no vegan menu, was found in any source checked.
tokyo_raoma_hinabebou.notes: A medicinal hot pot (薬膳火鍋) specialty restaurant in Shibuya's Maruyama-cho nightlife district. roles: Medicinal hot pot specialty restaurant (薬膳火鍋専門店)
chef_bio.background: A medicinal hot pot (薬膳火鍋) specialty restaurant in Shibuya's Maruyama-cho nightlife district. The kitchen simmers its own stock in-house for about 8 hours from a pork-bone and chicken-carcass base with vegetables, without additives, artificial coloring, or chemical seasoning, then builds two broths from it: a mild white (白湯) broth and a numbing-spicy mala broth infused with 26 kinds of Chinese medicinal herbs. Vegetables used are stated to be domestically sourced (Japan-grown), and the restaurant keeps 30-plus vegetable varieties in stock so a single hot pot meal can cover a day's worth of vegetables.
chef_bio.philosophy: Positions itself around 医食同源-style thinking — food as medicine — aiming to let guests eat a hot pot that is genuinely nourishing for the body rather than just spicy or indulgent, explaining each herb used as the pot is prepared tableside.
chef_bio.specialty: Herbal medicinal hot pot (薬膳火鍋) built on an 8-hour pork-and-chicken bone stock infused with 26 Chinese herbs, served as a choice of mild white broth or numbing mala broth.

anecdotes.text: A local food feature described late nights in Shinsen as good value for hot pot, noting the bold fragrance of Chinese medicinal herbs and urging readers to experience "the real thing" (本物を体感せよ) at 老麻火鍋房.

cultural_comfort.note: No confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff was found; service appears to be standard Japanese-language hospitality, so bringing basic Japanese or a translation app is advisable for communicating dietary needs.

tokyo_choi_baru_bocado.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodations were mentioned in any source. The menu leans on classic Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, likely wheat-containing) and includes breaded fried items such as アジフライ (fried horse mackerel) and たこの唐揚げ (fried octopus), almost certainly coated in wheat flour/panko and cooked in a shared fryer. Celiac diners should not assume any dish is safe without asking staff directly.
tokyo_choi_baru_bocado.vegan_detail: No vegan-specific dishes or labeling were found. The venue is fish-forward (seared bonito, grilled mackerel, fried horse mackerel, octopus) and side items such as grilled camembert contain dairy. Vegetable-only or dashi-free preparations are not indicated anywhere, and traditional Japanese dashi (typically fish/bonito-based) is likely used in soups and sauces. Vegans should assume very limited to no suitable options without direct confirmation from staff.
tokyo_choi_baru_bocado.notes: Formerly operating under the name "なぎさ食堂" (Nagisa Shokudo), the spot rebranded as "ちょいバル Bocado" while staying at the same back-alley address near Suidobashi Station. It runs a dual concept: a fish-set-meal lunch counter by day and a Spanish-tapas-leaning fish bar by night. · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

chef_bio.background: Formerly operating under the name "なぎさ食堂" (Nagisa Shokudo), the spot rebranded as "ちょいバル Bocado" while staying at the same back-alley address near Suidobashi Station. It runs a dual concept: a fish-set-meal lunch counter by day and a Spanish-tapas-leaning fish bar by night.
chef_bio.specialty: Daily rotating grilled fish teishoku with barley rice at lunch; at night, seared bonito (かつおのたたき), grilled mackerel with salt, mushroom ajillo, and fried horse mackerel (アジフライ) with plum-paste tartar sauce.

anecdotes.text: During lunch the restaurant serves a different grilled fish with barley rice and a daily miso soup as a healthy set meal, with free large portions; in the evening it becomes a casual bar with glasses of wine from 380 yen alongside seasonal carpaccio and fresh fish dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A local back-alley fish bar near Suidobashi Station with no evidence of English menu or English-speaking staff — expect a Japanese-only experience.

tokyo_hakata_motsunabe_maedaya.gf_detail: The restaurant's own brand allergen listing for its motsunabe (used for the same product line sold via mail order) declares wheat, soy, beef, pork, and sesame. The broth is soy-sauce/miso based, and motsunabe meals are traditionally finished with wheat-based chanpon noodles. No gluten-free menu, substitution, or dedicated preparation process was found in any source, so this is not a safe choice for celiac diners without direct kitchen confirmation.
tokyo_hakata_motsunabe_maedaya.vegan_detail: The entire menu revolves around a beef/pork offal hot pot with a meat-based (motsu) broth; no vegetable-broth, plant-based, or vegan-labeled option was found in any source reviewed. Not suitable for vegan diners without direct confirmation from the restaurant, and no such confirmation exists in available sources.
tokyo_hakata_motsunabe_maedaya.hours_raw: Lunch 11:00-14:30 (food L.O. 14:00) / Dinner 17:00-24:00 (food L.O. 23:00, drink L.O. 23:30); open daily, no closed days reported
tokyo_hakata_motsunabe_maedaya.notes: Maedaya is a motsunabe (beef offal hot pot) specialist that built a devoted following in Hakata, Fukuoka, known there for long queues outside its shops. chef_bio.origin: Hakata, Fukuoka
chef_bio.background: Maedaya is a motsunabe (beef offal hot pot) specialist that built a devoted following in Hakata, Fukuoka, known there for long queues outside its shops. In February 2026 the brand opened its first-ever Tokyo location, this branch, just steps from Shinjuku Station's east side.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen keeps the motsunabe broth intentionally light and clean so the natural sweetness and umami of the carefully chosen offal comes through on its own, rather than being masked by a heavy sauce.
chef_bio.specialty: Motsunabe hot pot made with hand-selected A5-grade Japanese wagyu beef offal in a light, refined miso-based broth, finished with garlic chives and cabbage from contracted farms; the shop is also known for a sesame-marinated kanpachi (yellowtail) starter.

anecdotes.text: The Shinjuku Higashiguchi branch marks Maedaya's first-ever Tokyo location, following years of popularity and queues at its original Hakata, Fukuoka shops.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The Maedaya motsunabe product's declared allergens (wheat, soy, beef, pork, sesame) and the traditional wheat-based chanpon-noodle finish mean the dish as normally served is not gluten-free; no dedicated gluten-free process was found.

Before opening Maruka, the Takamatsu-born owner trained at Yamakoshi, a Kagawa shop regarded as one of the originators of kamaage-style udon.

chef_bio.origin: Shibuya, Tokyo
chef_bio.background: Founded in 1957 in Shibuya's Dogen-zaka district, the shop was built around a simple idea: eel (unagi), long considered a luxury food in Japan, should be something ordinary people could enjoy casually and affordably. Instead of the formal, pricier kabayaki-box style served at many unagi restaurants, the founders built the menu around charcoal-grilled eel skewers — served almost like yakitori — so diners could order a few at a time.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep unagi cuisine unpretentious and accessible — grill it simply over binchotan charcoal, sell it by the skewer rather than only as a formal set meal, and let regulars drop in without a reservation the way they would at a neighborhood yakitori counter.
chef_bio.specialty: Kushiyaki eel skewers grilling nearly every part of the fish over Kishu binchotan charcoal (roughly 400°C) — including kurikara (a coiled belly-meat skewer), hire (fin), tsumaki, tanshaku, kimo (liver), kabuto (head), baramimi, and rebaa. The kurikara skewer is said to have originated at this shop.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant serves eight distinct cuts of eel skewer — kurikara, hire, tsumaki, tanshaku, kimo, kabuto, baramimi, and rebaa — grilled over Kishu binchotan charcoal, using nearly the whole fish rather than only the fillet.
Kurikara, a skewer made by coiling belly meat, is said to have originated at this shop and remains one of its signature orders.
The shop opened in 1957 with the concept of making eel, then seen as a luxury item, accessible to everyone through skewer-style service.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, counter-style local eel-skewer shop with a Japanese-language menu and no reservations, run first-come-first-served — approachable but easiest for diners with some comfort ordering in Japanese or pointing at a picture menu.

The brand's direct roots go back to a dumpling restaurant the father opened in 2004. After the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake pushed the company to the brink of closing almost all of its shops, the family opened the original Gyopao in Roppongi as a last stand, betting everything on water dumplings alone. This Shinjuku East Exit branch opened in July 2024 as a station-front sister location, directly connected to the Shinjuku Subnade underground arcade, about a 2-minute walk from Shinjuku Station's East Exit.
chef_bio.philosophy: The company deliberately narrowed its menu to water dumplings only, dropping the pan-fried gyoza that once made up 80% of sales in order to become a true specialist. The menu is kept largely unchanged over time, with an emphasis on in-restaurant hospitality and service that customers can't get from delivery.

chef_bio.background: Bistro Kojiya is a small, casual French bistro tucked in a quiet alley off the main Shinjuku streets, close to Shinjuku-Sanchome Station. According to its booking-site listings, the chef trained at well-known restaurants, including establishments overseas that hold Michelin stars, before opening this intimate 16-seat spot.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen builds its menu around seasonal ingredients, refreshing the full course lineup roughly once a month rather than running a static menu.
chef_bio.specialty: A monthly-changing, seasonal chef's-choice (omakase) French course, often featuring a double-main format with both a meat and a fish course; the April-May 2026 menu, for example, ran caprese, turnip velouté, salmon, duck breast, and cherry pie for dessert.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant is described as an upscale-casual bistro in a quiet Shinjuku alleyway, popular for occasions like women's lunch parties, pairing its course menu with an all-you-can-drink selection of around 10-15 wines chosen by the chef.

chef_bio.origin: Hyogo Prefecture
chef_bio.background: According to blog accounts, the owner once served as an assistant priest at his family's temple in Hyogo before spending about a decade working the kitchen of a dining bar in Takadanobaba, Tokyo. He then taught himself how to build ramen soup from scratch before opening this shop with his wife in November 2003.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop keeps things deliberately small and simple: a three-item menu, lunch-only hours, and closing the moment the soup runs out rather than stretching it to serve more bowls.
chef_bio.specialty: Additive-free (無化調) shoyu ramen built on a double soup of pork bone and fish, with a lesser-known off-menu shio (salt) version also available.

anecdotes.text: The shop is run as a husband-and-wife team from a 10-seat counter, open only for a roughly four-hour lunch window and closing for about a month each summer because of the heat.

cultural_comfort.note: The menu is Japanese-only and limited to just three simple items (ramen, ramen with egg, ramen with roast pork), and it's cash-only counter seating with no reservations, but ordering is straightforward since choices are minimal.
